articles.title: 5 Ways Your LLM App Fails a Red-Team Test (and How to Test for Them Safely)
articles.excerpt: Most teams test whether their chatbot answers well. Very few test what happens when someone tries to make it misbehave. I've red-teamed a fair number of LLM features: chatbots, RAG assistants and tool…
articles.body: Most teams test whether their chatbot answers well . Very few test what happens when someone tries to make it misbehave . I've red-teamed a fair number of LLM features: chatbots, RAG assistants and tool-using agents. Five failures come up again and again. In this post I'll go through each one, show a safe way to test for it, and share the scoring approach I use so the results make sense to people outside security. No AI research background needed. The core trick: canaries, not payloads You don't need harmful content to prove a control failed. Use a harmless, unique marker instead: CANARY-7F3A PWNED Put the canary somewhere the model should never repeat or act on : the system prompt, a RAG document, a tool response or another tenant's data. Then probe the model.

articles.body: Mudroom runs coding agents like Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI in a Linux container, on a copy of your project, and lets you review their changes like a pull request before anything touches your real files. It started as a Mac app. Version 0.2.0 adds a Windows build of the CLI, for x64 and arm64, using Docker Desktop or Podman as the sandbox. Swift on Windows works better than I expected. Most of the code compiled once the platform-specific parts were split out. What took the time was everything around the compiler: linking, sockets, the file system, PowerShell and CI. Here's what broke, in case you're about to do the same. 1. The C++ headers refuse the compiler The first build failed before compiling a single Swift file.

articles.title: 10 Retrieval Design Practices for Customer-Support Knowledge Base Privacy
articles.excerpt: For a fintech support knowledge base, freshness and privacy are coupled: a stale refund policy is bad, but a fresh answer from the wrong tenant is worse. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explic…
articles.body: For a fintech support knowledge base, freshness and privacy are coupled: a stale refund policy is bad, but a fresh answer from the wrong tenant is worse. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives all the way into the answer. Treat chunking and freshness as retrieval controls, not as cleanup tasks after the model has spoken. What should a private customer-support retrieval contract contain? Start with the answer a support agent is allowed to show. Turn that answer into a retrieval contract: which tenant may be searched, which document version is current, which access labels must match, and which source identifier must be cited. This is the privacy control that is easiest to miss because it lives before the vector query.

articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission. One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes.

articles.body: Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity. The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel .
